newsitem.title: CHINA: Former China defence minister dies, aged 82.
newsitem.headline: Former China defence minister dies, aged 82.

text.p: Former Chinese Defence Minister Qin Jiwei, a close associate of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping who helped to orchestrate the military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989, has died at 82.
Born in 1914, Qin died of an illness early on Sunday, the People's Daily said on Monday.
Qin still held the position of vice-chairman of the standing committee of China's National People's Congress, or parliament, at the time of his death but had retired from his other posts.

Appointed defence minister in 1988 and a member of the Communist Party's powerful Central Military Commission, Qin was a key player in Deng's decision to use the army to suppress student-led protests centred in Tiananmen Square in June 1989.

Qin's support as a close ally of Deng was essential in ensuring the backing of the military when Deng decided to impose martial law in Beijing in May 1989 and then send in troops, backed by tanks, to crush the protests with heavy loss of life.

The use of the army in the crackdown was opposed by some senior military leaders as well as lower-ranking officers who disagreed with deploying the army to tackle internal unrest, arguing that the military's role was defensive.

A native of Qiliping, in north China's Hebei province, Qin began his military career as a 13-year-old guerrilla in 1927. Two years later, his unit was absorbed into the communist army. He joined the party the following year.

He participated in the communist forces' famous Long March in 1934 and 1935. In the Sino-Japanese War from 1937 to 1945 and the Chinese civil war afterwards, he served as an army officer under the command of Deng.
In 1950 he commanded the 15th Army opposing United Nations forces in Korea.
He held important military regional commands until the ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution when he was persecuted as a follower of Deng.

He was a strict disciplinarian and a proponent of modernising China's armed forces, although as a loyal party member he has publicly supported Deng's policy of putting economic development before military spending.
Qin was rehabilitated in the mid-1970s and after commanding the Chengdu military area command in western China, was brought to Peking by Deng.
After Deng's ascent to power in the late-1970s, he became commissar and commander of the politically-sensitive Peking military area command.

He rose to defence minister in 1988, and became a member of the party's ruling politburo, the State Council, or cabinet, and the Central Military Commission, then chaired by Deng, which controls China's three-million-strong armed forces.
He enjoyed playing Chinese chess, and was honorary president of the Chinese Chess Association as well as honorary president of the Shooting Association of China.
